name: Spaghetti Standoff
summary: A ritual duel built from extreme scale contrast and accelerating rhythm. Establish the arena in extreme wide, set the duelists in a wide 50/50 two-shot that shows the empty ground between them, then cycle hip-height cowboy singles (gun hand in frame), close-ups, extreme close-ups of eyes and inserts of hands while each shot gets tighter and shorter and the score climbs. The draw itself goes back to the wide so cause and effect read in one frame. Duration is the weapon: the audience is made to wait.

editing: accelerating cut rhythm toward the draw
alternate scales EWS/ECU
inserts of hands, holsters, pocket watch
hold the release
match cuts on eyes across duelists
sound: wind, spurs, silence
score builds and cues the cuts
gunshot as release

rules.then: establish the whole arena and every duelist's position in one wide before any close-up
rules.why: tension needs geography: the audience has to know distances and lines of fire before it can fear the draw

rules.then: make each cycle of singles tighter (cowboy, then CU, then ECU eyes) and shorter than the one before
rules.why: shrinking size and duration raise arousal; eyes carry intention while hands carry capability

rules.then: keep each duelist's screen position fixed and reset with a neutral overhead or wide if the lines get confusing
rules.why: a three-way standoff has three axes of action; stable screen geography is the only thing stopping disorientation

rules.then: cut back to the wide two-shot or a cowboy shot for the draw itself
rules.why: the payoff must show cause and effect in one frame; a close-up draw hides who fired first

name: Bomb Under the Table
era: codified by Hitchcock in the 1930s-60s; universal suspense grammar since
summary: Suspense instead of surprise: show the audience the threat first, then make it watch people who do not know. Hitchcock's own example is a bomb under a table: let it go off unannounced and you buy a few seconds of shock; show it first and the most banal conversation becomes unbearable for minutes. The cutting does the work: a clean insert of the threat and its deadline, an ordinary unhurried scene played straight, and returns to the clock that come back sooner and tighter each time. Object size in frame tracks story importance, so the parcel is shot as big as a face. Decide the payoff deliberately; Hitchcock later regretted letting the bomb in Sabotage kill a boy the audience had been made to protect.

color: ordinary everyday palette: normality is the counterpoint
no warning color on the victims
editing: cross-cut threat and oblivious people
returns to the threat at shrinking intervals
clock or deadline inserts that visibly advance
hold the banal dialogue past comfort
sound: an audible tick or clock motif
banal dialogue played straight
score withheld or a low pulse

rules.then: show the threat in a clean, readable insert, including how long is left
rules.why: suspense is made of information: the audience can only dread what it has been shown

rules.then: make each return shorter and tighter and let the clock visibly advance
rules.why: shrinking intervals compress perceived time and pull the payoff toward the viewer

rules.when: staging the people who do not know
rules.then: keep them relaxed and their business ordinary, and hold their shots a little longer than feels comfortable
rules.why: the gap between their calm and our knowledge is the suspense; nervous characters close that gap

rules.then: defuse, escape or redirect unless killing an innocent the audience protected is the point
rules.why: an audience that has been made to guard someone feels cheated when the film punishes it for caring

name: Dolly Zoom
era: first used in Vertigo (1958, credited to Irmin Roberts); a standard shock device since Jaws (1975)
summary: The camera tracks and the zoom moves in the opposite direction at the same rate, so the subject stays the same size while the background perspective stretches away or crowds forward. Nothing in the subject changes, yet the space around them does, and the viewer reads that as the inside of a person lurching: a realization, a shock, vertigo. It needs real depth behind the subject (a street, a corridor, a stairwell) or the change is invisible, and it needs the subject's size locked or it reads as a sloppy zoom. Use it once, on the single biggest internal beat, framed by stillness before and after.

color: the grade of the surrounding scene: the effect should not announce itself through color
editing: static setup before, hold the reaction after
once per film or sequence
cut out as the move completes
sound: ambient sound drops out or thins
a low swell or ringing tone under the move

rules.then: center the subject on the lens axis and keep their size locked from first frame to last
rules.why: any drift in subject size makes it read as an ordinary zoom and the illusion collapses

rules.then: put deep space with strong parallel lines behind the subject
rules.why: perspective change is only visible where there is depth to stretch or compress

rules.then: precede it with a static or conventional shot and follow it with a held reaction
rules.why: contrast with stillness is what makes the space appear to move

rules.then: run it slowly, over two to four seconds
rules.why: a slow change feels like the world shifting; a fast one reads as a gag

name: One-Point Symmetry
era: classical architecture painting onward; Kubrick's signature from the 1960s to the 1990s
summary: All the lines of a set (walls, ceiling lights, floor) converge on one vanishing point at the center of a wide frame, the camera sits exactly on that axis, level, with no tilt, and a subject is placed on or against the axis. A slow, constant forward track down the corridor makes the space feel engineered and inevitable: the viewer is pulled toward a destination nobody chose. Kubrick used it across his career (Kogonada's supercut collects dozens of examples), pairing wide lenses with a head-lowered, eyes-up stare for menace. The effect is control, coldness and dread; humans look small and subordinate to the order of the space.

color: one saturated accent color in the set (red, orange)
editing: long holds on the symmetrical frame
cut from symmetry to symmetry
few cutaways
sound: classical or electronic score in counterpoint
room tone of machines and air handling

rules.then: put the lens axis on the vanishing point, camera exactly centered, horizon level and no tilt so verticals stay parallel
rules.why: any tilt makes the verticals converge and breaks the symmetry; an off-center camera reads as an accident rather than a design

rules.then: track forward or back along the axis at a slow, constant speed
rules.why: constant motion along the axis feels mechanical and inevitable; speed changes make it feel operated

rules.then: set the subject on the axis or deliberately just off it
rules.why: on axis reads as order and destiny; slightly off reads as something wrong in the order

rules.then: hold the face centered with the head lowered and the eyes raised to the lens, on a wide lens close in
rules.why: the frontal geometry plus the downward head makes the look feel aimed at the viewer

name: Planimetric Deadpan
era: Wes Anderson from the late 1990s; roots in silent comedy and in Kitano's flat staging
summary: The camera faces the back wall square-on, the frame is flat (planimetric) and the subjects are centered or arranged in a row like a diorama. Characters often face the lens and deliver lines without reaction pauses; the composition, not the performance, tells the joke. Instead of cutting, the camera whip-pans between people or trucks sideways along the set like a page turning, and information arrives through overhead inserts of hands and objects laid out flat. Pastel color blocking and chapter cards complete a storybook control that is funny and, underneath, melancholy: people pinned inside very neat boxes.

rules.why: the flat frontal plane is the joke's container; any diagonal turns tableau back into ordinary coverage

rules.why: the whip keeps both inside one continuous mechanical space and lands like a comic beat

rules.why: the top-down insert matches the planimetric world and reads like a page in a picture book

name: Blocking-Driven Oner
era: classical plan-sequence tradition; refined by Spielberg from the 1970s on
summary: A dialogue scene played as one moving take in which the coverage is hidden in the blocking. Actors move between depth planes and the camera makes small, motivated adjustments, so the frame recomposes itself through a master, a two-shot, a clean single and an over-the-shoulder without a cut. Unlike a showy Steadicam journey, the audience rarely notices it is a long take, because every resting frame is a shot an editor would have chosen anyway. Tony Zhou's essay on Spielberg's oners is the standard breakdown. The payoff is real-time performance and an unbroken sense of space; the cost is that the editor gets no cutting points, so the rhythm must be built on set.

color: the scene's naturalistic grade: the move should be invisible, not the look
editing: the take is the scene: no cutting points inside it
optional insert or reaction only after the take resolves
rhythm built through actor speed and camera pauses
sound: overlapping natural dialogue
score enters only after the take settles

rules.then: design it as a list of resting frames (master, two-shot, single, OTS) first, then block the actors to travel between them
rules.why: the take only feels invisible if every pause lands on a frame that would be a legitimate cut

rules.then: move only when an actor moves, and move less than they do
rules.why: motivated, smaller moves hide the camera; unmotivated moves expose the virtuosity

rules.then: use a wide-normal lens and stage in depth so actors change size by walking toward or away from the lens
rules.why: depth staging produces close and wide sizes without zooms or long dolly moves

rules.then: shoot a safety insert or a reaction that can be cut in only at a natural pause
rules.why: a single long take leaves no way to fix pace or a flubbed line otherwise

name: Awe Face Push
era: Spielberg from the mid-1970s; now standard blockbuster grammar
summary: Before the audience sees the wonder, it sees a face seeing it. A close-up of wide eyes and an open mouth, lit by interactive light from the unseen thing, with a slow push-in; the object is withheld for a beat or several, so the face and the audience's imagination build it up. Then the reveal: an extreme wide, often from low or behind the character, with a human figure in frame for scale. Then back to the face. Kevin B. Lee's 2011 video essay named it the Spielberg face. It works because emotion transfers from faces before information arrives, and because withholding lets the viewer's expectation do half the work.

editing: face first, object second, face again
hold the withheld beat longer than expected
reveal in the widest size of the scene
sound: sound drops to a hush before the reveal
score swells on the reveal, not before

rules.then: show the face reacting, with a slow push, for at least one beat before the object appears
rules.why: the face tells the audience how to feel and the delay lets expectation build

rules.then: go to an extreme wide with at least one human figure in frame
rules.why: scale only reads against a known size; without a person the wonder has no measure

rules.then: let light from the unseen thing fall on the face and change over the shot
rules.why: interactive light proves the object is real and present before it is shown

rules.then: move slowly and stop before the shot ends
rules.why: a slow push reads as being drawn in; a fast one reads as alarm

name: Tatami Low Static
era: Yasujiro Ozu, late 1920s to 1962; widely homaged in slow and family cinema
summary: A locked-off camera placed low, around the eye level of someone kneeling on a tatami floor (the exact height and the reason are debated; roughly 0.6-0.9 m), nearly always on a 50mm. Dialogue is shot as matched frontal singles with eyelines just off the lens, close to direct address, and Ozu happily cuts across the 180-degree line so the room becomes a 360-degree space. Scenes are joined not by dissolves but by pillow shots: empty rooms, laundry, chimneys, a train passing. The style refuses to steer the viewer. With nothing moving, small domestic gestures carry enormous weight, and the pillow shots give time for feeling to settle.

silvery black and white in the earlier films
editing: straight cuts only: no dissolves, fades or wipes
pillow shots bridge scenes
matched frontal singles that cross the 180-degree line freely
sound: ambient: trains, clocks, wind, cicadas
gentle score that enters between scenes

rules.then: set it low, at kneeling eye height, level, and lock it off
rules.why: the low level-headed view is the style's calm, respectful vantage; moving it makes it ordinary coverage

rules.then: use matched frontal singles at the same size with eyelines just off the lens, cutting directly between them
rules.why: near direct address puts the viewer in the conversation and equal sizes keep any judgment out

rules.then: use one or more pillow shots of empty spaces or objects instead of a dissolve
rules.why: the empty frames hold the emotional aftertaste and mark time without commentary

rules.then: cross it freely when it gives a better frontal composition, as long as each frame is self-contained
rules.why: this grammar treats each frame as a composed picture rather than part of a continuous screen geography

name: Step-Print Smear
era: Hong Kong, 1990s (Wong Kar-wai and Christopher Doyle); widely imitated in music video
summary: Shoot undercranked, around 8-12 frames per second with a long shutter so every frame carries a streak of motion blur, then step-print: duplicate each frame (two to three times) to return to 24 fps. Motion keeps roughly its real speed but stutters and smears. Put a lead who moves slowly or holds still inside a fast crowd and the crowd dissolves into streaks of neon while the person stays legible: time feels split between them and the world. Doyle shot it handheld on wide lenses in real Hong Kong streets lit by signage. It is a subjective, romantic device for isolation, longing and memory, used in short bursts inside otherwise normal-speed scenes. For AI generation it is largely a frame-rate effect: describe the long blur trails in the prompt and emulate the stutter in post by holding frames.

rules.why: the smear only reads as subjective time when something in frame holds its shape against it

rules.then: undercrank to about 8-12 fps with a long shutter and step-print back to 24 fps
rules.why: the long shutter supplies the streaks and the duplicated frames supply the stutter; one without the other looks like an error

rules.then: use it in short bursts at moments of feeling, not as the scene's default
rules.why: contrast with normal-speed footage is what makes it read as a shift in the character's experience

name: Nape Follow
era: Dardenne brothers from the late 1990s; extended in Son of Saul (2015)
summary: A handheld camera stays close behind a character, at neck height, so the back of the head and the nape fill a third or more of the frame and the world is glimpsed past an ear or a shoulder. The face is withheld for long stretches. The viewer shares the character's pace, blind spots and urgency but cannot read their expression, so they are forced to infer motive from posture and action; empathy comes without access. It is the signature of Dardenne social realism (natural light, no score, real locations), and Son of Saul pushed it further with shallow focus that leaves the horrors around the protagonist blurred. When the face is finally shown, frontal, it lands as a revelation.

editing: long takes that end on an action, not a line
abrupt cuts to black
no reaction coverage
sound: diegetic only: breathing, footsteps, traffic
no score

rules.then: stay close behind at neck height so the back of the head fills a large part of the frame
rules.why: proximity puts the viewer in the character's body; at a distance it becomes ordinary surveillance

rules.then: react to the character rather than anticipate them, arriving a beat late at each turn
rules.why: a camera that lags reads as a witness sharing the risk; one that leads reads as an author who knows the plot

rules.then: withhold the frontal face until a story beat earns it
rules.why: the long denial turns the first full look at the face into a payoff

rules.then: keep it diegetic, with no score telling the audience how to feel
rules.why: music would supply the inner state the withheld face deliberately leaves open

name: Motivated Locked Camera
summary: The camera is locked off on sticks or a remote head and moves only when an actor moves, and then exactly as much: a tilt that matches a sit-to-stand, a pan that starts and stops with a walk, a dolly that keeps pace with a stride. Because no movement is ever unmotivated, the camera feels like an impassive observing system, not an operator, which gives scenes a cold, inevitable precision. Fincher pairs it with many takes for exact timing, clean low-noise digital darkness, a desaturated sodium-yellow and fluorescent-green palette, and occasional locked overhead shots that look down on characters like specimens before something terrible happens.

editing: cut on the end of a matched move
precise, invisible continuity
overhead shot as a tonal warning
sound: low ambient drone
dialogue clean and close

rules.then: move the camera in exact proportion and duration, starting and stopping with the actor
rules.why: matched motion makes the camera feel like an automatic system rather than an operator, which is the source of the coldness

rules.then: keep the camera perfectly still
rules.why: any unmotivated drift breaks the contract that the camera only responds

rules.why: the god's-eye view turns the person into a specimen and signals that something is about to happen to them

rules.then: stay on sticks or a stabilized remote head even in tense scenes
rules.why: the tension comes from control, not from shake

name: Three-Way Standoff
era: Leone's cemetery triello (1966), Hong Kong heroic bloodshed (late 1980s), Tarantino (1990s)
summary: Three armed players, each covering one or both of the others, so the scene has three axes of action instead of one and the editor's main job is keeping geography readable. Establish the triangle in one frame (a high wide or an overhead) before any single. Lock each player to a screen position and keep every single consistent with it: A frame-left looking right, B frame-right looking left, C upstage looking toward the lens between them. Cycle singles, inserts of hands and weapons, and the three-shot, cutting faster and tighter as the moment approaches, and reset with a neutral overhead whenever anyone moves. The release goes back to the wide so the audience can see who fired at whom.

rotate singles in a fixed order, then break the order
neutral overhead reset
release in the wide
sound: silence, breathing, hammers cocking
score or a single sustained tone climbing

rules.then: show all three positions in one high wide or overhead before cutting to any single
rules.why: with three axes of action, the audience must see the triangle once or every eyeline afterward is ambiguous

rules.then: keep each player on a fixed screen side with a fixed eyeline direction, and put the upstage player near frontal so they can look toward either partner
rules.why: consistent screen geography is the only thing that tells the viewer who is covering whom

rules.when: someone moves or the lines shift
rules.then: cut to a neutral overhead or the triangle wide to re-establish before resuming singles
rules.why: a reset gives the viewer a fresh map instead of a tangle of crossed lines

rules.then: shorten and tighten the singles as the moment approaches, then cut back to the wide for the shots themselves
rules.why: acceleration raises arousal; the wide shows cause and effect in one frame
